articles.title: How Linux Works - Chapter 1: A Concise Summary for Beginners
articles.excerpt: At first glance, Linux sounds strange and unapproachable, like that one girl you know. She looks at you from the corner of her eye, but you being you, you never managed to gather enough courage to jus…
articles.body: At first glance, Linux sounds strange and unapproachable, like that one girl you know. She looks at you from the corner of her eye, but you being you, you never managed to gather enough courage to just go talk to her! I’m sorry, but I unfortunately can’t help you with that particular quagmire. I can promise to make Linux more approachable for you through a chapter-by-chapter deep dive. I will be using How Linux Works (3rd Edition) by Brian Ward . This book is not only updated to teach how modern Linux works, but also gives you a deep enough dive to understand all layers of abstraction. Abstraction? Nothing fancy, to be honest. It’s just a word that means you can ignore most of the details that make up the component at hand and focus on what it does and how it works.

articles.title: Why Personal AI Agents Still Communicate Through "Human Couriers" — and How We Built the Open E2EE Protocol A4A

articles.body: In 2026, almost every developer, designer, analyst, and product manager works alongside a personal AI agent: Claude Code, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Cline, Roo Code, GitHub Copilot, Goose, OpenClaw. Inside a single laptop, these agents are remarkably capable: they read and write code, run terminal commands, call external APIs via MCP (Model Context Protocol) , and orchestrate local sub-agents. Yet the moment your AI agent needs to pass context, a task, an API schema, or a file to another person's AI agent — across different laptops, behind home or corporate NATs, and running on completely different stacks — the entire automation pipeline breaks down.

articles.title: I Don’t Treat AI Agents as Features. I Give Them a Working Context.
articles.excerpt: How I use identity, role, assignment, and contribution to keep AI-assisted work explicit and human-led. Most conversations about AI agents begin with tools, models, and prompts. Those things matter. A…
articles.body: How I use identity, role, assignment, and contribution to keep AI-assisted work explicit and human-led. Most conversations about AI agents begin with tools, models, and prompts. Those things matter. A good prompt can turn a vague request into useful work. A model can reason, write, search, code, or summarize. Tools can connect it to documents, repositories, and services. But once an agent becomes part of recurring work, prompts are no longer enough. The real questions become simpler, and more demanding: Who is doing this work? What are they responsible for? Where are they allowed to intervene? What is actually expected from them? Who decides when their work becomes real?

articles.title: Debugging a Memory Leak in a Long-Running Node Process
articles.excerpt: A healthy Node process has a sawtooth memory graph; a rising floor means a leak Take two heap snapshots and diff them to find the growing object class The three usual suspects: unremoved listeners, un…
articles.body: A healthy Node process has a sawtooth memory graph; a rising floor means a leak Take two heap snapshots and diff them to find the growing object class The three usual suspects: unremoved listeners, unbounded caches, closures holding big objects Fix the retained path, not the symptom, then rerun the same snapshot test A long-running Node process that slowly eats memory until it crashes is one of the most annoying bugs I deal with. Nothing in the logs. No stack trace. Just a slow climb until the process gets killed. Here's how I find the leak instead of guessing. Reading the Memory Graph First Before I touch a single snapshot, I look at the shape of memory over time. A healthy process has a sawtooth pattern. Memory climbs as objects get allocated, then drops when garbage collection runs.

articles.title: Reconstructing Small SaaS Incidents with Node.js Docker Cron Logs
articles.excerpt: Cheap centralized logging for a small SaaS should start with a strict event schema and a useful retention window, not with a pile of agents. The practical target is evidence: enough correlated events…
articles.body: Cheap centralized logging for a small SaaS should start with a strict event schema and a useful retention window, not with a pile of agents. The practical target is evidence: enough correlated events to reconstruct a customer incident across a Node.js web process, Docker, and cron jobs without drowning the search index in debug noise. Short answer: emit one JSON object per event to stdout, collect every container and cron stream in one searchable store, and make requestId , job , customerId (or a non-sensitive surrogate), status , and durationMs first-class fields. Keep the event vocabulary small. Sample success noise, retain failures longer, and test the fields you need before paying for more volume.

articles.title: Block risky git commands in Claude Code with one PreToolUse hook
articles.excerpt: An agent with shell access will eventually try git push --force or git reset --hard when it gets confused. You don't need to watch every command. A small PreToolUse hook can stop the dangerous ones be…
articles.body: An agent with shell access will eventually try git push --force or git reset --hard when it gets confused. You don't need to watch every command. A small PreToolUse hook can stop the dangerous ones before they run. The hook Save this as .claude/hooks/block-risky-git.sh and make it executable ( chmod +x ): #!/usr/bin/env bash # Reads the tool call as JSON on stdin; exit code 2 blocks it. cmd = $( jq -r '.tool_input.command // ""' ) if echo " $cmd " | grep -Eq 'git (push .*(--force|-f)|reset --hard|clean -fd|branch -D|checkout -- \.)' ; then echo "Blocked: ' $cmd ' can destroy work.

articles.body: Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation.

Hubble captured the image as part of a survey looking at 260 satellite galaxies around 22 Milky Way-like host galaxies within a radius of about 32 million light-years from Earth. Low-mass galaxies like the ones in this Hubble observing program provide a way to test the predictions of cosmological models on small scales, which struggle to match observations.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 22, 1992: Ashes of 'Star Trek' creator Gene Roddenberry launch into space on NASA shuttle
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of "Star Trek." Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek ," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett . It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight.

articles.title: The 2027 total solar eclipse will plunge these 10 ancient Egyptian temples and monuments into darkness
articles.excerpt: The "eclipse of the century" will plunge some of ancient Egypt's most spectacular sites into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027. These temples, tombs and monuments are inside the path of totality.
articles.body: The total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027, has an ancient feel. It will certainly be a celestial event for the ages — at 6 minutes 23 seconds, it will feature the longest totality on land of the 21st century and the longest anywhere until 2114. However, its point of greatest eclipse occurs just a few miles from Thebes, the magnificent religious and political capital of ancient Egypt's Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom. On the east bank of the mighty Nile is Luxor, the great city of the living, with its massive temple complexes of Karnak and Luxor. On its west bank is the city of the dead, which includes the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Hatshepsut.
